item.title: (Calā): Having been born, one must die, Seeing suffering in birth, Fetters and afflictions — Therefore I do not delight in birth. The Buddha has…
item.description:
(Calā):
Having been born, one must die,
Seeing suffering in birth,
Fetters and afflictions —
Therefore I do not delight in birth.
The Buddha has taught the Dhamma
That leads beyond renewed existence,
Abolishing all suffering —
He has established me in truth.
Beings headed for the form realm,
Those aspiring to the formless realm,
If they do not know cessation,
They go to renewed existence.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.6

item.title: “Householder, just as a house with a badly thatched roof — the ridgepole is not protected, the rafters are not protected, the walls are not…
item.description:
“Householder, just as a house with a badly thatched roof — the ridgepole is not protected, the rafters are not protected, the walls are not protected; the ridgepole becomes soaked and leaks, the rafters become soaked and leak, the walls become soaked and leak; the ridgepole rots, the rafters rot, the walls rot. So too, householder, when the mind is not guarded, bodily actions are not guarded, verbal actions … mental actions … then bodily actions become soaked with greed and leak, verbal actions become soaked with greed and leak, mental actions become soaked with greed and leak. For one whose bodily actions are soaked and leak with greed, whose verbal and mental actions are soaked and leak with greed, bodily actions rot, verbal actions rot, mental actions rot. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions rot, death is not good, the end is not good.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.109

item.title: Life is swept along, The lifespan is short — Led to old age, There is no shelter. Seeing this danger in death, Always do meritorious…
item.description:
Life is swept along,
The lifespan is short —
Led to old age,
There is no shelter.
Seeing this danger in death,
Always do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.
Here, restraint of body,
Restraint of speech and mind —
One who does this, even while dying,
Experiences happiness,
Because while still alive,
He has made merit.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.51

item.title: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind…
item.description:
“Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — regarding them, my mind becomes inflamed when they are present, and diminishes when they are future, not yet attained.’ Then, monks, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — regarding them, for my own benefit, I will dwell heedful, protecting my mind with mindfulness.’ Therefore, monks, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure that your minds formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — your minds become inflamed when they are present, and diminish when they are future, not yet attained. Therefore, monks, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure that your minds formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — for your own benefit, dwell heedful, protecting your minds with mindfulness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.117

item.title: All formations are impermanent, Having arisen, they must cease; Having arisen, they are subject to cessation, Their calming is bliss.
item.description:
All formations are impermanent,
Having arisen, they must cease;
Having arisen, they are subject to cessation,
Their calming is bliss.

From: Dīgha Nikāya 16 – Mahāparinibbānasutta

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who do not know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who do not know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in the case of forms — they will certainly not understand forms as they actually are, nor can they lead others to a similar position, namely, understanding forms as they actually are — such a thing is not possible. Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in the case of forms — they will certainly understand forms as they actually are, and they can lead others to a similar position, namely, understanding forms as they actually are — such a thing is possible.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is the practice of restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the practice of restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the eye faculty, practices restraint of the eye. When he hears a sound … smells an odor … tastes a flavor … feels a touch … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the mind faculty, practices restraint of the mind. This, monks, is called the practice of restraint.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.164

item.title: “Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of gross personality view. If you practice accordingly, then defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and…
item.description:
“Poṭṭhapāda, I teach the Dhamma for the removal of gross personality view. If you practice accordingly, then defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, you realize and abide in full, vast wisdom. Poṭṭhapāda, you might think: ‘Defiling states will be abandoned, pure states will increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in full, vast wisdom — yet suffering still remains.’ Poṭṭhapāda, do not think thus. When defiling states are abandoned, pure states increase, and in this very life, by direct knowledge, one realizes and abides in full, vast wisdom — then gladness arises, joy, tranquility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and a pleasant abiding arise.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 9 – Poṭṭhapādasutta

item.title: “Form is a lump of glowing ember, monks! Feeling is a lump of glowing ember! Perception is a lump of glowing ember! Formations are lumps…
item.description:
“Form is a lump of glowing ember, monks! Feeling is a lump of glowing ember! Perception is a lump of glowing ember! Formations are lumps of glowing ember! Consciousness is a lump of glowing ember! Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.136

item.title: Standing to one side, a deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Among us humans, Sensual pleasures are impermanent. Whoever enjoys…
item.description:
Standing to one side, a deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Among us humans,
Sensual pleasures are impermanent.
Whoever enjoys them here,
Is tied, bound by them.
Heedless regarding them,
Hard to escape from them —
One who cannot escape easily
Is conquered by Death.
Danger arises from sensual desire,
Suffering arises from sensual desire.
If sensual desire is subdued,
Then danger is subdued,
When danger is subdued,
Suffering is subdued.
The various objects in the world
Are not the sensual desires themselves —
It is the thought of greed
That is the sensual desire of humans.
The various objects remain
As they are in the world,
Therefore the wise
Subdue their sensual desires.
Abandon anger,
Subdue conceit,
Overcome all
Fetters that bind.
Do not cling excessively
To that name-and-form —
Suffering cannot reach
One who has nothing.
Give up calculations,
Do not chase after false thoughts,
Cut off all craving
For name-and-form in the world.
That one, free from defilements,
Without anxiety, without craving —
Gods and humans,
In this life or the next,
In heavenly realms
Or any dwelling place,
Seeking but not finding
The trace of that one —
They search but do not see
The one thus liberated.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.34
